sections.html:
• Scientific name: Saron marmoratus
  • Other names: Marbled shrimp, Long Arms Marbled Shrimp, Monkey Shrimp, Eyespot Shrimp, Carid Shrimp, Buffalo Shrimp
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Water type: salt water, SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Diet: omnivore, mostly carnivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Coral safe: no
  • Colour: can change colour

Saron marmoratus is one of the most colourful and unusual-looking shrimp in the marine aquarium trade. It is hardy and easy to care for, so it can be recommended even to beginners. It can change colour to blend into its surroundings and avoid predators.

The family placement of this species is disputed: it is classified as a "cleaner shrimp" of the family Thoridae, but some authorities consider it a member of the family Hippolytidae sensu lato. The genus Saron contains 4 species that can look very similar to an untrained eye, especially when small, and the trade often uses the same names for different species.

There is a lot of conflicting information about corals. Some aquarists report Saron shrimp as completely reef safe for years, but there are also multiple reports of shrimp that were model citizens until they were caught picking at Zoanthid, Montipora and Pocillopora corals, Red Hornets, Bubble Tip Anemones and others. Saron shrimp are known to eat the polyps of a wide variety of hard and soft corals. They are not voracious eaters but can do it, especially if hungry. They should therefore not be listed as reef safe, rather as reef safe with caution.

Some say Saron marmoratus should not be confused with Saron recticostris (thick beige bodies with purple legs), which is not reef safe and can even attack duster worms, snails and other crustaceans.

Saron marmoratus is widely distributed across the Indo-West Pacific, from Hawaii, the Marquesas and Tahiti southward to Australia, and westward to the Malay Archipelago and across the tropical Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the east coast of Africa. It has also been reported from Agatti Island (Lakshadweep, India), eastern Australia, Iran and the Red Sea.

These shrimp are common among coral and coral rubble, in the infralittoral to sublittoral zone, down to a maximum depth of about 37 metres.

In nature, Saron shrimp can also be found at cave entrances near long-spined sea urchins. Although this is not a symbiotic relationship, in some experiments the shrimp followed the urchin when it moved. The shrimp use the long spines as protection; the benefit to the urchin is yet to be discovered.
At least a 10-gallon (40 litre) tank is needed for one shrimp, plus 5 more gallons (20 litres) for every additional shrimp. A larger tank is always preferable for the stability of water chemistry.

• Temperature: 22–26°C
  • pH: 8.1–8.4
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH
  • Calcium: 400–450 ppm is optimal; calcium, pH and alkalinity must be kept at acceptable levels

Saron marmoratus is a hardy species with no special water quality requirements; it should be kept under conditions suitable for any typical marine aquarium.

Lighting: Saron shrimp are nocturnal and very shy and generally do not need light at all, so lighting should be adapted only to the needs of the corals and other animals in the tank.

Substrate: they are not diggers and have no preference for the substrate.

Decorations: decorations provide hiding places (shelter and protection) and reduce stress, which is also extremely important for moulting. The tank should include plenty of structures to hide in.

Acclimation: acclimate the shrimp carefully for a few hours before adding them to the tank. Do it very slowly to avoid unnecessary stress.

Saron shrimp are natural scavengers. They are omnivores and opportunistic eaters that sift through the fine substrate at night looking for organic detritus, plankton, dead animals and other edible items. In an aquarium they are an effective part of the clean-up crew, feeding on debris, waste and rotting food.

Foods they will enjoy:

  • brine shrimp
  • scallop
  • mussel
  • mysis shrimp
  • plankton
  • flaked food
  • frozen food
  • small pieces of fish or shrimp

Saron shrimp are very shy and skittish. They do not like to be touched or handled. They are nocturnal and spend most of their time hiding under rocks. This is common among grazing invertebrates, because in nature it is mainly associated with avoiding visual predators while feeding. Once settled, they become slightly more outgoing and come out more often, even in the daytime.

This is generally a quite inactive species and can sit doing nothing for hours, but when threatened it becomes surprisingly fast, with an incredibly quick reaction time.

They also rely on camouflage: at night the body turns primarily red, a defence to hide from predators at twilight, while during the day they often become greenish to mottled brown and white.

They are not very social but tolerate others of their species. It is recommended to keep one male with one or two females.

  • Socialisation: low to medium
  • Activity: low
  • Active: at night
  • Peaceful: yes

Tankmates should be chosen with care. Many aggressive marine species will see them as prey, for example tangs, clownfish, triggerfish, puffers, larger hawkfish, larger wrasses, morays and lionfish. Aggressive eaters and large or aggressive invertebrates such as coral banded shrimp and arrow crabs should be avoided. Potentially good tankmates that usually do not bother Saron shrimp include boxer crabs, emerald crabs, porcelain anemone crabs, cleaner shrimp (peppermint shrimp, red fire shrimp, skunk cleaner shrimp, red-white cleaner shrimp), sexy shrimp and bumblebee shrimp.

It is rather difficult to tell male and female Saron shrimp apart. Scientifically, females can be distinguished as follows:

  • the dorsal margin of the carapace and the abdomen have tufts of setae, denser in females;
  • the first pereopod differs between the sexes and is shorter in the female;
  • females have an obvious brush-like structure of setae on the first pair of legs, whereas males have elongated chelae that are longer than the body.

Research on this species is limited. Some aquarists believe Saron shrimp are usually collected in pairs and form a monogamous relationship; otherwise they may fight to the death.

It is extremely hard to breed Saron shrimp in captivity, and there have been no reports of successful breeding in home aquariums. The pet industry depends completely on wild-caught animals.

According to a study, Saron marmoratus passes through several zoea and postlarva stages before metamorphosing into a small copy of the adult. Zoea and postlarvae require filtered seawater with a salinity of 35–37‰ and pH 7.9–8.1 at room temperature (23–26°C). In laboratory conditions, Artemia nauplii were offered as food.

Most articles say Saron shrimp grow to about 5 cm, but this is not accurate: they are fairly large, bigger than other "cleaner shrimp", and can easily reach about 8 cm or more.

In 1916 the marine zoologist Stanley Wells Kemp wrote that the "coloration of living specimens is very wonderful, resembling that of a rich Turkey carpet". The body is light brown and slightly greenish with yellow, marbled and white speckled spots and banded red and white legs. Each shrimp shows considerable individual colour variation, and the colour also varies from one location to another. There are feathery appendages, called cirri, on the back. The rostrum is relatively large, slightly longer than the carapace and strongly recurved. The abdomen is humped and a little longer than the carapace. The eyes are pear-shaped, large and prominent, and the walking legs (pereopods) are thin and hairy.

Lifespan: there is no data on the lifespan of Saron marmoratus in the wild, but in captivity it can live for 3 years if properly cared for.
